Build a full-3D, explorable recreation of the Heeler family home from the animated series Bluey: the house, the garden around it, and the four members of the family. The scene is still: nothing moves except the visitor's camera. The visitor walks around the garden, climbs to the veranda, enters the house, and meets the family.

Everything is built in code from Three.js geometry and procedural materials. The goal is a place a fan of the show recognizes at first glance, in the show's flat, bright, rounded cartoon style.
</instructions>

<core-experience>
The page is one fullscreen 3D scene, a small help panel, and a compact location label.

- The visitor starts in the garden, standing on the grass, facing the house, with the whole front of the house and at least one family member in view.
- The visitor can walk all the way around the house, go up the stairs to the veranda, enter the house through an open doorway, and walk from room to room.
- Nothing in the scene is animated: no idle motion, no swaying leaves, no moving clouds, no day-night cycle. Only the camera moves.
- The location label always names where the visitor is: `Garden`, `Veranda`, or the name of the room.
</core-experience>

<the-house>
The house is a raised timber Queenslander, as in the show.

- It stands on stilts, with an open space under the floor that the visitor can see into from the garden.
- Timber walls, a pitched corrugated metal roof, windows on every side, and a wide veranda with railings along the front.
- Stairs lead from the garden up to the veranda. The visitor climbs them by walking; the camera follows the steps up and down.
- An open doorway leads from the veranda into the house.
- Inside, at least three connected rooms the visitor can walk through: a living room with a couch and a rug, a kitchen with a bench, and the girls' bedroom with two beds. Add more rooms if you want.
- Furnish every room so it reads as a lived-in family home: toys, cushions, pictures on the walls, kitchen objects. Pick the details yourself.
</the-house>

<the-garden>
- A large backyard of grass that slopes gently, with the house in it. The ground is not a flat plane.
- A big shade tree in the yard, large enough to stand under.
- At least four other garden features of your choice that fit the show's backyard (play equipment, a fence, plants, outdoor furniture, toys left on the grass).
- A sky and distant surroundings that close the scene: the visitor never sees the edge of the world or an empty void.
</the-garden>

<the-family>
The four Heelers stand or sit in the scene, each in a still pose of your choice:

- Bluey: a blue heeler puppy, six years old.
- Bingo: a red heeler puppy, four years old, smaller than Bluey.
- Bandit: the dad, a blue heeler, the tallest of the four.
- Chilli: the mum, a red heeler, shorter than Bandit, taller than Bluey.

Rules:

- Each character is recognizable on its own: body colors and markings, ear shape, muzzle, tail, eyes. Use the show's colors as you remember them.
- Characters stand upright on two legs in the show's proportions: big heads, short bodies.
- Size order, tallest first: Bandit, Chilli, Bluey, Bingo.
- Place at least one character outside and at least one inside the house.
- Each character stands on a floor, a step, the grass, or furniture. No character floats or sinks into a surface.
- When the visitor is within 1.5 m of a character and looking at it, a small label shows the character's name.
</the-family>

<navigation>
- Walk mode (default): first-person view at a child's eye height of 1.0 m above the surface under the visitor. Mouse look with pointer lock after a click on the scene; W A S D or arrow keys to move; Shift to move faster.
- Walking speed: 2 m/s, and 4 m/s with Shift.
- The visitor cannot walk through walls, furniture, the tree trunk, the stilts, the railings, or the characters. Moving into one slides along it instead of stopping dead.
- The visitor follows the height of the ground, the stairs, and the floors. No flying, no falling through the ground.
- Orbit mode: press O to switch to an orbit camera around the whole property (drag to rotate, wheel to zoom), and O again to return to walk mode at the last walking position.
- The help panel lists the controls and can be hidden with H.
</navigation>

<rendering>
- Three.js, loaded from a pinned CDN version. three/addons from that same version are allowed.
- Flat, bright, cartoon colors with soft daylight: one sun with a shadow map, plus soft fill light. All characters, the house, the tree, and the furniture cast and receive shadows.
- Indoor rooms are lit well enough to see every object.
- No external image, model, HDR, texture, or font file. Generate any texture in code.
- Steady frame rate on a recent laptop: merge or instance repeated geometry where it helps.
</rendering>

<inspection>
Expose `window.sceneState()`. It returns a plain JSON object with:

- `camera`: `{ mode, position: [x, y, z], yaw, pitch }`, where `mode` is `walk` or `orbit`, positions are in meters, and angles in degrees
- `location`: the text currently shown in the location label
- `characters`: an array of four objects `{ name, position: [x, y, z], height, location }`, where `height` is the character's standing height in meters and `location` is where it is placed (`Garden`, `Veranda`, or a room name)
- `rooms`: the names of the rooms inside the house
- `landmarks`: the names of the garden features you built
</inspection>

Use a walking-skeleton approach: start by writing a minimal end-to-end version of index.html, then grow it in small increments until the page is complete.

- Do not open a browser.
- Do not click the page.
- Do not run the page to visually test it.
- Do not iterate after a preview.

Build a full-3D roller coaster: a train of cars climbs a chain lift, drops, runs through a vertical loop, an airtime hill, and a banked turn, then brakes back into the station.

This is a simulation, not a scripted animation. Once the train leaves the lift chain, its speed at every point must come out of forces integrated step by step along the track: gravity, and friction or air drag when they are on. Never set the speed from a formula of the height, and never move the train along a precomputed timeline.
</instructions>

<core-experience>
The page is one fullscreen 3D scene, a control bar, a settings panel, and a live readout.

- On load, the train waits in the station and dispatches by itself at t = 1 s, without any click.
- It rides the whole circuit and stops in the station, then waits.
- Dispatch (button or D key) sends the train again with the current settings.
- If the train cannot crest a hill, it stops on the slope and rolls back under gravity, exactly as the simulation dictates. The readout shows "Rollback" and the element where it happened. Reset (button or R key) returns the train to the station.
</core-experience>

<track>
The track is one closed circuit made of these elements, in this order. Heights are those of the track centerline above flat ground.

1. Station: flat, at 2 m. Brakes hold the train while it waits.
2. Chain lift: a straight incline. The chain pulls the train up at a constant speed and lets it go at the crest. The crest height is a setting.
3. First drop: from the lift crest down to 2 m.
4. Vertical loop: a teardrop loop, 26 m tall, from 2 m at the bottom to 28 m at the top. The top of the loop is a circular arc of radius 8 m. Riders are upside down at the top.
5. Airtime hill: a camelback hill whose crest is at 30 m. The crest is a circular arc of radius 15 m in the vertical plane.
6. Banked turn: a 180° turn of radius 20 m, flat at 6 m. Bank it so that, on the default ride, riders feel almost no sideways push.
7. Brake run: back down to 2 m, where brakes slow the train and bring it into the station.

Shape the transitions between elements yourself. The track must be smooth: no kinks in direction, no sudden jumps in curvature large enough to show as a spike in the g-force readout.

Build the track from a continuous centerline curve. Draw the two running rails, the ties, and the supports down to the ground.
</track>

<train>
- A train of cars, coupled, following each other on the track at a fixed spacing. Each loaded car weighs 500 kg.
- Simulate the train as one body moving along the track: its state is its distance along the track and its speed. The train's reference point is its middle; the height used for the physics is the track height under that point.
- The cars stay on the rails everywhere, including upside down and on a rollback: running wheels, side wheels, and upstop wheels hold them.
- Riders are visible in every seat.
</train>

<default-experiment-values>
These defaults are mandatory. They must be the initial values on first load so every implementation rides the same baseline circuit.

- Gravity: 9.81 m/s²
- Lift crest height: 40 m
- Chain speed: 3 m/s
- Cars: 6, at 500 kg each
- Rolling friction: off. When on: friction force = 0.015 × the normal force between the wheels and the rails, opposite to the motion
- Air drag: off. When on: air density 1.225 kg/m³, drag coefficient 0.9, frontal area 1.5 m² for the whole train, drag force ½ ρ Cd A v² opposite to the motion
</default-experiment-values>

<settings>
A settings panel is required. Every visible control must change the next ride. If a control is on screen, it is wired.

- lift crest height, 25 to 50 m
- chain speed, 1 to 6 m/s
- number of cars, 1 to 8
- rolling friction on / off
- air drag on / off
- gravity, with presets Earth 9.81, Mars 3.71, Moon 1.62

Changing a setting rebuilds the track if needed and puts the train back in the station.
</settings>

<live-readout>
Show these values while the train moves, measured from the simulation:

- speed (m/s and km/h) and height (m)
- vertical g-force felt by the riders: the force from the seat on a rider along the rider's own up direction, divided by the rider's weight. 1 at rest in the station, above 1 when pressed into the seat, below 0 when lifted out of it
- lateral g-force felt by the riders, sideways in the rider's own frame
- energy bars: kinetic, potential, and dissipated by friction and drag, and their sum

After each ride, show: maximum speed, maximum and minimum vertical g, ride time from dispatch to stop, and "Completed" or "Rollback" with the element where it happened.
</live-readout>

<playback-and-camera>
- Pause / Play, and simulation speed 0.25×, 0.5×, 1×. Space toggles pause unless an input is focused.
- Cameras: Front seat (the view of a rider in the first car), Chase (follows the train from behind and above), Orbit (drag to orbit around the whole park). Default is Chase. Switching does not reset physics.
</playback-and-camera>

<rendering>
- Three.js, loaded from a pinned CDN version. three/addons from that same version are allowed.
- Physically based materials: painted steel track and supports, cars, riders, ground.
- A shadow map on the sun light; the track, the supports, and the train cast shadows.
- Generate the environment in code or with Three.js RoomEnvironment. No external HDR, model, or texture file.
- The park around the coaster, the colors, and the atmosphere are your choice.
</rendering>

<physics>
- Fixed physics timestep with a cap on steps per frame.
- No Math.random in the physical setup or the force computation.
- The same settings give the same ride on reload and on Dispatch.
- Slow motion changes the clock, not the physical result.
</physics>

<inspection>
Expose `window.coasterState()`. It returns a plain JSON object with:

- `train`: `{ phase, element, distance, speed, height, gVertical, gLateral }`, where `phase` is `station`, `lift`, `free`, `brake`, or `rollback`, `element` is the name of the track element under the train's reference point, `distance` is in meters along the track from the station
- `energy`: `{ kinetic, potential, dissipated }` in joules, potential measured from the ground
- `track`: `{ length, elements: [{ name, start, end }] }`, with `start` and `end` in meters along the track
- `lastRide`: `{ maxSpeed, maxG, minG, speedAtDropBottom, speedAtLoopTop, gAtLoopTop, speedAtHillCrest, gAtHillCrest, maxLateralGInTurn, rideTime, completed, rollbackElement }` in SI units, or `null` before the first ride ends. `rollbackElement` is `null` when the ride completed
- `settings`: the current values of every control
</inspection>

Build a full-3D Foucault pendulum: a heavy bob hangs from a long wire under the dome of a great hall, swings across a graduated floor dial, and its plane of swing slowly turns because the Earth rotates under it.

This is a simulation, not a scripted animation. The bob's motion must come out of forces integrated step by step in the frame of the floor, which turns with the Earth: gravity, the wire tension, the Coriolis effect, and air drag when it is on. Never rotate the plane of swing yourself, never set it from a formula of the latitude or of the time, and never move the bob along a precomputed path.
</instructions>

<core-experience>
The page is one fullscreen 3D scene, a control bar, a settings panel, and a live readout.

- On load, the bob is held to the north side of its rest point by a thread. At t = 1 s the thread burns and the bob is released, without any click.
- The pendulum then swings on its own. The plane of swing turns over time, clockwise seen from above in the northern hemisphere, counterclockwise in the southern hemisphere, not at all at the equator, exactly as the simulation dictates.
- Release (button or L key) releases the bob when it is held. Reset (button or R key) puts the bob back on its thread at the release point and resets the simulated time.
- Changing a setting resets the pendulum. The bob then waits on its thread for Release.
</core-experience>

<hall-and-pendulum>
- The pivot is fixed under the top of a dome. The wire hangs straight down from it. The wire length is a setting; the hall is tall enough for the longest wire.
- The bob is a brass sphere, 0.38 m in diameter, at the end of the wire. Wire length is measured from the pivot to the center of the bob.
- The wire is rigid in length and has no mass. The pivot is ideal: no friction, no preferred direction.
- The bob moves in full 3D around the pivot: it is a spherical pendulum, not a planar one.
- The release point is due north of the rest point, at the release distance from it measured horizontally. The bob is released at rest relative to the floor.
- On the floor, centered under the pivot: a circular dial graduated every degree, labeled every 10°, with the four compass points. North on the dial is true north for the simulation.
- A ring of 36 small pins stands on the dial, one every 10°, at 0.9 × the release distance from the center. A pin falls over when the bob touches it, and stays down until Reset.
- A floor trace: the path of the bob's lowest point, drawn on the floor like a stylus in sand, fading over time, with an on / off toggle.
</hall-and-pendulum>

<earth-rotation>
- The simulation runs in the frame of the floor, with axes east, north, and up at the pendulum's latitude.
- In that frame, the only effect of the Earth's rotation is the Coriolis acceleration −2 Ω × v, where v is the bob's velocity and Ω is the Earth's rotation vector expressed in that frame: magnitude 7.2921 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s times the rotation multiplier, pointing toward the celestial north pole. The centrifugal effect is already included in g.
- The rotation multiplier exaggerates the Earth's rotation for teaching. At ×1 the Earth turns at its real rate.
</earth-rotation>

<default-experiment-values>
These defaults are mandatory. They must be the initial values on first load so every implementation swings the same baseline pendulum.

- Latitude: 48.8462° N
- Gravity: 9.81 m/s²
- Wire length: 67 m
- Bob mass: 28 kg
- Release distance: 3 m
- Rotation multiplier: ×1
- Air drag: off. When on: air density 1.225 kg/m³, drag coefficient 0.47, frontal area of the 0.38 m sphere, drag force ½ ρ Cd A v² opposite to the bob's velocity relative to the floor. The wire has no drag.
</default-experiment-values>

<settings>
A settings panel is required. Every visible control must change the next swing. If a control is on screen, it is wired.

- latitude, −90° to 90°, with presets Paris 48.8462, North Pole 90, Equator 0, Sydney −33.87
- wire length, 10 to 100 m
- bob mass, 5 to 50 kg
- release distance, 0.5 to 5 m
- rotation multiplier: ×1, ×10, ×100, ×1000
- air drag on / off
- gravity, with presets Earth 9.81, Mars 3.71, Moon 1.62
</settings>

<live-readout>
Show these values while the pendulum swings, measured from the simulation:

- simulated time since release, as hours, minutes, and seconds
- number of swings, and the period measured on the last full swing
- azimuth of the plane of swing: its direction in degrees clockwise from north, between 0 and 180
- precession rate: how fast the plane of swing turns, in degrees per hour of simulated time, fitted on the azimuths measured since release; positive when it turns clockwise seen from above. Also show the time this rate would take for a full turn
- current amplitude, and the closest distance between the bob and the rest point during the last pass
- energy bars: kinetic, potential, and dissipated by drag, and their sum
</live-readout>

<playback-and-camera>
- Pause / Play, and simulation speed 0.25×, 1×, 60×, 600×, 3600×. Space toggles pause unless an input is focused. At every speed the physics is the same.
- Cameras: Hall (a view of the whole pendulum from the floor of the hall), Overhead (looking straight down at the dial from under the pivot, north up), Orbit (drag to orbit around the pendulum). Default is Hall. Switching does not reset physics.
</playback-and-camera>

<rendering>
- Three.js, loaded from a pinned CDN version. three/addons from that same version are allowed.
- Physically based materials: brass bob, steel wire, stone hall, dial, pins.
- A shadow map on the main light; the bob, the wire, and the pins cast shadows.
- Generate the environment in code or with Three.js RoomEnvironment. No external HDR, model, or texture file.
- The architecture of the hall, the colors, and the atmosphere are your choice.
</rendering>

<physics>
- Fixed physics timestep with a cap on steps per frame. The cap must still let 3600× run in real time.
- No Math.random in the physical setup or the force computation.
- The same settings give the same swing on reload and on Reset then Release.
- Slow motion and time-lapse change the clock, not the physical result.
</physics>

<inspection>
Expose `window.pendulumState()`. It returns a plain JSON object with:

- `bob`: `{ phase, east, north, up, speed }`, where `phase` is `held`, `swinging`, or `paused`, and `east`, `north`, `up` are in meters from the rest point
- `swing`: `{ count, period, azimuth, precessionRate, fullTurnHours, amplitude, missDistance }`, with `period` in seconds, `azimuth` in degrees clockwise from north between 0 and 180, `precessionRate` in degrees per hour of simulated time, positive clockwise seen from above, `amplitude` and `missDistance` in meters. Fields are `null` until they can be measured
- `time`: `{ simulated }`, in seconds since release
- `energy`: `{ kinetic, potential, dissipated }` in joules, potential measured from the rest point
- `pins`: `{ standing, fallen }`
- `settings`: the current values of every control
</inspection>

Build a full-3D Rube Goldberg machine: a chain reaction where each stage triggers the next one only through physical contact, simulated by a real 3D rigid-body engine. The chain has nine stages in a fixed order. Eight are specified below; the ninth is your own invention. Theme the machine and the room freely.

This is a simulation, not a scripted animation. If a physical parameter makes a stage fail, the chain must stop there, and the page must say which stage failed.
</instructions>

<core-experience>
The page is one fullscreen 3D scene, a compact control bar, and a stage checklist.

- The machine fits on a large workbench or a room floor, about 4 m long. Stages are laid out so every one is visible from the overview camera.
- The default run starts by itself one second after the page loads. Do not require a click before the chain starts.
- When the bell rings, the page shows the total chain time in simulation seconds and holds on the finished machine.
- Replay rebuilds a fresh run from the current settings. The first automatic run must use the mandatory defaults exactly.
</core-experience>

<mandatory-chain>
The stages run in this order. Each stage starts only when a body from the previous stage touches it. No timers, no scripted triggers, no teleporting bodies between stages.

1. Release gate: a steel ball rests behind a gate at the top of a ramp. The gate swings open at t = 1 s. This is the only timed event in the whole machine.
2. Switchback ramps: the ball rolls down a first ramp, then down three more ramps that zigzag downward, each one reversing the ball's horizontal direction. The ball must stay on the ramps by contact with side rails, not by a guiding constraint.
3. Dominoes: the ball leaves the last ramp and hits the first of 24 dominoes. The domino line includes one 90° turn. Each domino falls because the previous one hits it.
4. Lever: the last domino pushes a heavy block off a shelf. The block falls onto the short arm of a seesaw lever. The long arm flips up and launches a light ball.
5. Pulley: the light ball lands in a basket hanging from a rope that runs over a fixed pulley to a counterweight. At rest, the counterweight sits on the floor, which holds the empty basket up. The loaded basket is heavier than the counterweight, so the basket goes down and the counterweight lifts off the floor. The rope keeps a constant length.
6. Pendulum: the descending basket presses a latch that releases a pendulum held at 60° from vertical.
7. Newton's cradle: the pendulum bob strikes the first ball of a five-ball Newton's cradle. The last ball of the cradle swings out.
8. Your stage: the last cradle ball triggers one stage of your own invention. It must be physical, visible, and different from every other stage in this list (no second set of dominoes, no second pendulum). It must end by touching the bell's striker.
9. Bell: a striker hits a bell. The bell rings with a sound generated by the Web Audio API, and the chain is complete.
</mandatory-chain>

<default-experiment-values>
These defaults are mandatory. They must be the initial values on first load so every implementation runs the same baseline machine.

- Gravity: 9.81 m/s²
- Steel ball: radius 0.03 m, mass 0.11 kg
- Ramp slope: 20°
- Domino size: 0.20 m tall × 0.10 m wide × 0.03 m thick
- Domino mass: 0.15 kg
- Domino spacing (center to center): 0.12 m
- Heavy block on the shelf: 1.0 kg
- Lever: total length 1.0 m, pivot 0.25 m from the short end
- Light ball launched by the lever: 0.05 kg
- Empty basket: 0.20 kg
- Counterweight: 0.22 kg
- Pendulum: length 1.0 m, bob mass 0.5 kg, released from 60°
- Newton's cradle: 5 steel balls, radius 0.025 m, restitution 0.95
- Friction between ball and ramps: 0.3
</default-experiment-values>

<settings>
A settings panel is required. Every visible control must change the next run when the user hits Replay or Apply. If a control is on screen, it is wired.

Required live controls:

- gravity
- domino spacing
- domino mass
- counterweight mass
- pendulum length and release angle
- lever pivot position
- Newton's cradle restitution

These settings must produce physical consequences, not scripted ones:

- A gap between two dominoes (spacing minus thickness) larger than the domino height: the domino line stops.
- Counterweight heavier than the loaded basket: the basket does not go down.
- Changing the pendulum length moves its pivot so the bob still meets the cradle at the bottom of its arc. A longer pendulum takes longer to reach the cradle.
- Lower cradle restitution: the cradle transfers less motion, and the chain may stop.
</settings>

<stage-checklist>
Show a compact list of the nine stages. Each stage lights up when it triggers, with its trigger time in simulation seconds.

If no stage triggers for 8 simulation seconds after the previous one, mark the waiting stage as failed and show a short message naming it.

Show these measured values, read from the simulated bodies, not computed from a formula:

- the basket's acceleration during its descent, in m/s²
- the pendulum's swing time, in seconds, from its release to its impact on the cradle
</stage-checklist>

<playback-and-camera>
- Pause / Play, freezing physics and the clock. Space toggles pause unless an input is focused.
- Simulation speed: 0.25×, 0.5×, 1×. The selected speed survives Replay.
- Cameras: Overview (whole machine), Follow (moves automatically to the active stage), Orbit (drag to orbit). Default is Follow. Switching does not reset physics.
</playback-and-camera>

<rendering>
- Three.js, loaded from a pinned CDN version. three/addons from that same version are allowed.
- Physically based materials: metal balls with reflections, wood dominoes, rope, a brass bell.
- A shadow map on the main light; all moving bodies cast and receive shadows.
- Generate the environment in code or with Three.js RoomEnvironment. No external HDR, model, or texture file.
- Give the room and the machine a coherent theme of your choice. Decorations must not touch the chain.
</rendering>

<physics>
- Use a real 3D rigid-body engine loaded from a CDN, such as Rapier, cannon-es, or ammo.js.
- Fixed physics timestep with a cap on steps per frame.
- No Math.random in the physical setup or the collision response.
- The same settings produce the same chain on reload and on Replay.
- Slow motion changes the clock, not the physical result.
</physics>

<inspection>
Expose `window.machineState()`. It returns a plain JSON object with:

- `stages`: an array of nine objects `{ id, name, status, triggeredAt }`, where `status` is `waiting`, `triggered`, or `failed` and `triggeredAt` is a simulation time in seconds or `null`
- `basketAcceleration`: the measured value in m/s², or `null`
